lines.text: From a flicker of people in a garden to the shows the whole world streams at once. This is the story of film and television, told one picture at a time.
It starts with a magician. Georges Melies, a Paris stage conjurer, saw that a camera could do tricks too, and filled his films with vanishing acts and painted worlds.
In 1888, in a garden in Leeds, Louis Le Prince filmed two seconds of people strolling about. It is the oldest film we can date, and its maker soon vanished without a trace.
The next year a boy was born in London who would become the Tramp. Charlie Chaplin went on to make the whole world laugh, and sometimes cry.
In Lyon the Lumiere brothers filmed their own workers going home. Shown to a paying crowd in Paris in 1895, it is often counted as the birth of cinema.
So began the age of silent film: no recorded voices, just title cards and a live pianist, for more than thirty years of growing skill.
A year later the Lumieres filmed a steam train rolling into a station. Legend says the audience ran from it. Historians doubt that, but it shows the thrill of motion.
In 1899 Alfred Hitchcock was born in London. He would become the master of suspense, and a famous face in his own films, if only for a moment.
In 1902 Melies fired a capsule from a cannon straight into the eye of the Moon. A Trip to the Moon was one of the first science fiction films ever made.
A year later, in America, The Great Train Robbery cut from scene to scene to tell one story of outlaws and a posse, and the Western was on its way.
In 1910 Akira Kurosawa was born in Tokyo. His samurai epics would one day carry Japanese cinema to audiences around the world.
After the First World War, Germany made The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, all crooked sets and sharp shadows, and horror films have looked a little like it ever since.
In 1921 Satyajit Ray was born in Calcutta. A director, a writer and a composer, he would bring Bengal's quiet lives to the world's screens.
Then came Nosferatu, an unauthorised Dracula with a rat-like vampire. A court ordered every copy destroyed, but a few survived, and so did the legend.
In the Soviet Union, Sergei Eisenstein made Battleship Potemkin. Its massacre on the Odesa steps, built from fast cuts, taught the world what editing could do.
In 1927 Fritz Lang built Metropolis, a towering city where workers toil below the rich. Its robot still shapes science fiction, and lost footage turned up in Argentina in 2008.
That same year The Jazz Singer let audiences hear a few songs and lines on screen. Within a few years silent pictures were over.
In 1931 sound came to Hindi films in Mumbai, and Bollywood was born, with romance, family and action wrapped in song and dance.
Chaplin held on to silence a little longer. In Modern Times his Tramp is swallowed by the machines of a factory in the Great Depression.
In 1937 Walt Disney gambled on a full length cartoon. Hollywood expected Snow White to fail, but it made animated features a lasting business.
In 1939 a tornado carried Dorothy from black and white Kansas into the bright Technicolor of Oz, and generations would watch her find the way home.
The same year brought Gone with the Wind, a vast Civil War epic and a huge success, though its rosy picture of the Old South is now widely criticised.
In 1941 Orson Welles told the life of a newspaper tycoon through other people's memories. Citizen Kane changed how films were shot, and critics still call it the best.
Meanwhile the shadows deepened. Film noir filled the forties and fifties with tough detectives, dangerous women and streets lit from below.
In wartime, Casablanca asked a nightclub owner to choose between love and the cause. It won best picture, and people are still quoting it.
In Italy, as the war ended, film makers took cameras into ruined streets and cast ordinary people. Neorealism showed life as it was, and the world took notice.
Now television arrived. Every Sunday night The Ed Sullivan Show brought acts of every kind into American homes, from Elvis Presley to the Beatles.
In Latin America, radio serials became the telenovela, a daily romance with a planned ending that the whole world would come to watch.
In 1951 Lucille Ball began scheming her way into show business in I Love Lucy. Shot on film before a live audience, it gave us the rerun.
The next year, Singin' in the Rain looked back fondly on the scramble from silence to sound, and Gene Kelly danced through a downpour.
In 1953 the United States approved a standard for colour television. Other countries followed in the sixties, and black and white sets slowly faded away.
That year in Japan, Yasujiro Ozu made Tokyo Story, about old parents whose busy children have no time for them. Quiet and still, it is counted among the greatest films.
Then Kurosawa made Seven Samurai, poor villagers hiring warriors to fight off bandits. Westerns and action films have been borrowing its story ever since.
In 1955 Satyajit Ray made his first film, Pather Panchali, a village childhood in Bengal. It brought Indian art cinema to the world's attention.
In the late fifties, young French critics like Godard and Truffaut picked up cheap cameras, shot in the streets and broke every rule. This was the French New Wave.
On American television, Rod Serling opened the door to The Twilight Zone, strange little tales with twist endings and sharp things to say about prejudice and war.
In 1960 Hitchcock checked a woman into a lonely motel. The shower scene in Psycho shaped horror films for decades, and late arrivals were not let in.
In 1963 the BBC launched Doctor Who, a time travelling alien who changes face, and actors, when badly hurt. After a long pause it returned in 2005.
In 1966 Star Trek set off to explore the galaxy with a mixed crew unusual for its time. Cancelled after three seasons, it found its audience in reruns.
As the old studio system faded, young directors like Coppola and Scorsese got rare freedom. New Hollywood made personal, often dark films for more than a decade.
In 1968 Stanley Kubrick took us from the first apes to a voyage to Jupiter, with a computer that turns on its crew. 2001 changed what space on film could look like.
The next year, six comedians in Britain threw out the punchline. Monty Python's Flying Circus made television comedy strange, surreal and very silly.
Also in 1969, Sesame Street set out to get young children ready for school, with Muppets and short lessons that were soon copied around the world.
In 1972 Coppola's The Godfather told of a crime family handing power from father to son, and set a new standard for serious drama.
That year also brought MASH, a comedy about army surgeons in Korea made in the Vietnam years. Its final episode drew a record audience.
In the summer of 1975, a shark called Jaws emptied the beaches and filled the cinemas. Steven Spielberg had invented the blockbuster.
In Britain, John Cleese ran a hotel very badly in Fawlty Towers. Only twelve episodes were made, yet it is still called one of the best comedies ever.
Then Jim Henson's puppets took over a theatre. The Muppet Show welcomed a new guest star each week and made Kermit and Miss Piggy famous everywhere.
In 1977 Roots followed one African American family from capture in West Africa through slavery to freedom. Over eight nights, a whole nation watched and talked.
That same year a farm boy, a princess and a smuggler took on an evil empire. Star Wars changed Hollywood's effects, its toys and its business.
On the small screen, a Texas oil family feuded through Dallas, and the question of who shot the main character kept much of the world guessing.
In 1979 David Attenborough traced the whole history of life in Life on Earth, setting the model for the great nature series to come.
A year later Carl Sagan took viewers across the universe in Cosmos, and hundreds of millions of people came along.
In 1981 Hill Street Blues wove many stories through each episode with a shaky, news-like camera, and prime time drama was never quite the same.
The next year Spielberg returned with a lonely boy and a gentle alien who just wants to go home. E.T. became the biggest film of its time.
Also in 1982, Blade Runner sent a detective after artificial humans through a rainy future Los Angeles. A modest hit then, its look shapes science fiction still.
In Japan, Oshin told one poor girl's life from childhood to old age. Its story of perseverance was a record hit across Asia and beyond.
In India, the epic Ramayan came to Sunday morning television, and streets emptied as millions gathered around their sets.
In 1989 Seinfeld made comedy out of tiny everyday annoyances, a show about nothing that became one of the most watched of the nineties.
That same year a yellow family from Springfield arrived. The Simpsons is still running, the longest American scripted series in prime time.
In 1990 David Lynch sent an FBI agent to a small northwestern town to solve a murder. Twin Peaks showed how dreamlike television could be.
In 1993 Spielberg brought dinosaurs back to life with computers. Jurassic Park changed how films were made, and earned more than any before it.
Meanwhile in Nigeria, films shot fast and cheap on video and sold on cassettes grew into Nollywood, one of the largest film industries on Earth.
On television, two FBI agents chased the unexplained in The X-Files, and science fiction thrillers became mainstream.
That same year Spielberg made Schindler's List in black and white, the story of a German businessman who saved more than a thousand Jewish people from the Holocaust.
In 1994 Quentin Tarantino shuffled linked crime stories out of order in Pulp Fiction. It won at Cannes and made independent film a major force.
Disney answered with The Lion King, a young lion who flees his kingdom and returns to claim it, a huge hit that later became a stage musical.
And six friends moved into New York apartments. Friends ran ten seasons, and people are still watching it today.
In Japan, Neon Genesis Evangelion put teenagers in giant machines, then turned inward to their troubled minds. It is one of the most discussed anime ever.
In 1995 Pixar made Toy Story, the first feature made entirely by computer, and proved that such films could tell a story with real heart.
Two years later James Cameron sank the Titanic once more, around a love story. It won eleven Oscars and for years was the highest earning film ever.
In 1998 a company began posting DVDs to people's homes. Netflix would later stream films over the internet and change how the world watches.
The next year, a New Jersey mob boss began seeing a therapist. The Sopranos showed television could rival film, and a new golden age began.
That spring, The Matrix told a hacker his world was a simulation. Its bullet time fights were copied everywhere.
In 2001 Hayao Miyazaki drew a girl lost in a bathhouse of spirits. Spirited Away won the Oscar for animation and topped Japan's box office for years.
That winter, Peter Jackson's Fellowship of the Ring set out from New Zealand, proving long fantasy novels could be filmed on an epic scale.
In 2002 The Wire turned its eye on Baltimore, its police, dealers, docks, schools and papers, and critics have studied it ever since.
In 2006 Planet Earth filmed the world's wild places from the air in high definition, with rare animals few had ever seen.
A year later Mad Men took us into 1960s advertising offices, and became the first basic cable series to win the Emmy for best drama.
Then a New Mexico chemistry teacher with cancer turned to making drugs. Breaking Bad's five tight seasons are often named the best ever made.
In 2009 James Cameron took us to the moon Pandora with new 3D cameras. Avatar became the highest earning film ever, and 3D cinema boomed.
In 2011 Game of Thrones set noble families fighting for one throne, and became one of the most watched and awarded dramas on television.
By now streaming ruled. In 2016 Stranger Things sent children of the eighties against monsters from another dimension, a huge hit for Netflix.
That same year in Japan, Makoto Shinkai's Your Name swapped a city boy and a country girl into each other's bodies, and Asia flocked to see it.
From Spain came Money Heist, a mastermind robbing the national mint. On Netflix its red jumpsuits and masks spread across the world.
In 2019 Avengers Endgame closed a story told across twenty two Marvel films, and for a while it was the highest earning film ever.
That year South Korea's Parasite, Bong Joon-ho's dark tale of a poor family in a rich house, became the first non English film to win best picture.
Two years later Korea struck again. Squid Game turned children's games deadly, and became one of the most watched series Netflix ever had.
In 2022 Cameron went back to Pandora and into its oceans, and The Way of Water became one of the highest grossing films ever.
The summer of 2023 turned pink. Greta Gerwig's Barbie left her perfect world for the real one, and became the biggest film of the year.
Released the same weekend, Oppenheimer told of the scientist behind the atomic bomb, and won seven Oscars including best picture.
In 2024 Pixar returned to a teenage girl's mind, where Anxiety took the wheel. Inside Out 2 was the biggest film of the year.
And in 2025 China's Ne Zha 2, about a mythical boy hero, became the highest grossing animated film of all time.
From a garden in Leeds to screens in every pocket, the pictures keep moving, and we keep watching.
